readerContract.humanQuestion: What do I need to understand about AI, from the physical infrastructure through models, products, work and public consequences, so I can use it deliberately and recognise what a confident claim leaves out?
readerContract.promisedPayoff: The reader gains one connected foundational map, a separate direct-lookup route and a set of precise questions that help her use AI at work and home, test important claims and contribute to decisions without borrowing somebody else's confidence or jargon.
readerContract.priorKnowledge: No engineering, coding or AI vocabulary is assumed. The reader only needs to recognise an ordinary task, product, workplace proposal or headline that uses the label AI.
readerContract.centralMentalModel: AI is not one object. Physical infrastructure enables training and use; training shapes a model; inference applies a trained model to current input; products add context, instructions, retrieval, tools, permissions and interfaces; workflows and institutions determine how outputs become actions; evidence and accountable human decisions determine what should be trusted or done.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: Short work, home and public-discussion situations reveal different parts of the same system: using an assistant for a real task, deciding what information it can use, questioning an automation proposal and reading claims about chips, energy, jobs, evidence or public services.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A durable, revisable, book-like explanation that works as six connected chapters plus a separate Concept Index for direct lookup. It is not a class transcript, provider catalogue, current product manual, news digest or glossary wall.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I can finally see how the pieces fit together. I know which part a claim is about, what evidence or limitation matters and what useful question I can ask next.

Build a connected causal learning arc and keep the reader's judgment central.
Use warm, funny, practical language without hiding the mechanism.

Do not inherit factual or product claims without current evidence.
Do not turn a durable book into an episode transcript.

strengthsToUse: Answer the reader's actual question early.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: AI literacy means seeing the whole chain behind the label: physical infrastructure makes computation possible; training produces a model; inference uses it; products add information, tools, permissions and interfaces; organisations turn outputs into actions; evidence and accountable people decide what should be trusted or done.
causalSequence: Chips, servers, networks, data centres, electricity, cooling, capital and labour make computing capacity possible.
Training data, objectives, evaluation choices and computing work shape a model before the reader's present task.
During inference, the trained model processes the current input and produces a result appropriate to its model type.
A product assembles instructions, current context and permitted retrieval or tool results around the model.
Workflows and agents may repeat model and tool steps, but permissions, stopping rules, monitoring and accountability remain designed outside the model.
People and institutions decide where outputs enter work, markets or public services and who can contest an error or consequence.
The reader locates a claim in this chain, checks its evidence and date, names what is missing and chooses the next useful question or action.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: The representative proof starts with the famous strawberry letter-counting question. It shows the exact o200k_base pieces `st | raw | berry`, then traces ordinary text to token pieces, model processing and readable output. The case explains why fluent language and letter-by-letter inspection are different jobs without claiming that every current model fails the question.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: Without a supplied solution, the reader sees a product advertise a 100,000-token context window. She explains that this is a capacity measured in model input/output pieces rather than 100,000 words, says why the exact word equivalent varies and asks what material the product actually includes in the window and how well it uses material near the limit.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: When an AI feature, output, workplace proposal or headline matters, ask: Which layer is this claim actually about? What information, permission or evidence shapes the result? What changed between training and this use? What important person, cost, uncertainty or consequence is missing? Who retains authority and what evidence would change the decision?

analogyPlan.analogy: Making a sentence from words and word-pieces cut from a stack of old magazines: sometimes a useful word arrives whole and sometimes it must be assembled from smaller scraps.
analogyPlan.mapping: The magazine scraps map to a tokenizer's fixed reusable text pieces; their order maps to the sequence the model receives; assembling the scraps back into a sentence maps to converting generated tokens into readable text.
analogyPlan.limit: A tokenizer is not choosing scraps by meaning, taste or appearance. It follows a fixed encoding, and another encoding may cut the same text differently. Tokens are not little ideas or guaranteed word parts.
analogyPlan.whyItHelps: The uneven scraps make it immediately visible that a token is not necessarily one word or one letter, which explains the strawberry example and prepares the reader to understand context measured in tokens.

humourPlan.lessonJob: A brief spelling-bee observation after the mechanism makes the mismatch memorable: a model can be dazzling at prose while letter counting asks it to recover detail hidden inside its usual pieces. The line must not say that current models universally fail or turn the reader into the joke.

draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: Introduction: why practical and civic AI literacy matters and how to use the chapters plus Concept Index. Chapter 1: physical infrastructure—chips, servers, data centres, networks, electricity, cooling and compute. Chapter 2: how models are made and used—data, training, evaluation, inference, tokens, generative AI and other model types. Chapter 3: what the system has now—context, context window, sessions, memory and retrieval. Chapter 4: what surrounding software can add—tools, permissions, APIs, MCP, routing, wrappers and harnesses. Chapter 5: multi-step work—workflows, agents, sub-agents, skills, loops, monitoring and stopping. Chapter 6: why results and claims fail—grounding, hallucination, oversimplification, verification, evidence, contestability and human decision. Then a separate Concept Index with stable anchors, one-line meanings, chapter locations and explicit system relationships.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: The book body is one connected explanation, not a repeated entry set. Chapters use different explanatory forms because their mechanisms differ. The Concept Index performs compact recognition and routing only. Communication dimensions are outcomes to earn, not seven compulsory subheadings or a copied Hannah Fry format.

communicationDesign.surfaceAdaptation: Apply the communication mechanics to a scannable, resumable Library book. Use question-led chapter openings, concrete cases, deterministic diagrams and return questions where they reduce mental work; do not reproduce the pacing, performance, personality or structure of a television talk, lecture or Hannah Fry book.

humanQuestion.reason: Tokens matter when the reader encounters context limits, usage charges or an oddly difficult letter-level task; the section must answer why the term affects real use rather than merely define it.
humanQuestion.plannedEvidence: Open with the familiar question about the three r's in strawberry and the puzzle of why a fluent language model can find a letter-counting task unexpectedly awkward.

usefulCuriosity.reason: The contrast between a person's visible letters and a model's input pieces opens a precise gap that tokenization resolves.
usefulCuriosity.plannedEvidence: Ask the reader to look at strawberry as letters, then reveal the labelled `st | raw | berry` split used by one current OpenAI encoding.

invisibleProcessConcrete.reason: Tokenization happens before model processing and is normally invisible in a chat interface.
invisibleProcessConcrete.plannedEvidence: Use one deterministic live-text diagram: `you type strawberry` → `one named encoding makes st | raw | berry` → `the model processes the ordered pieces` → `generated pieces become readable text`.

familiarTechnicalMovement.reason: The strawberry example and magazine-collage analogy must lead into the correct token mechanism and then return to context, price and letter-level tasks.
familiarTechnicalMovement.plannedEvidence: After the visual, define tokens plainly, name where the collage analogy stops and show exactly what changes when a product quotes a token window or an API meters token use.

limitationsConsequences.reason: A useful explanation must not turn one encoding or a viral failure into a universal claim about every model or every language.
limitationsConsequences.plannedEvidence: State that splits vary by encoding and language, tokenization contributes to character-level difficulty but does not determine every answer, and current limits/prices must be checked in current product documentation.

humourSurprise.reason: The surprising gap between polished prose and spelling-bee mechanics is memorable and adult when the humour follows the explanation.
humourSurprise.plannedEvidence: Let the reader count the letters with no calculator, emergency meeting or tiny reading glasses, then use the magazine-clipping analogy only to make variable-size pieces visible; do not mock the learner or claim every current model loses the strawberry spelling bee.

betterNextQuestion.reason: The reader needs a reusable question when a product advertises a token limit or an answer depends on exact text.
betterNextQuestion.plannedEvidence: End with two precise moves: ask what the product counts inside the token window, and ask for a character-by-character check or an appropriate tool when exact spelling matters.

explanationArc.sharedStartingPoint: The reader can see three r's in strawberry and has probably seen the viral question about why a powerful language model could make this look difficult.
explanationArc.curiosityGap: How can software that writes a polished paragraph handle a tiny spelling job differently from a person looking at the letters?
mechanismSequence: The reader types visible text, but software first segments it according to one tokenizer and encoding.
That encoding turns the text into an ordered sequence of reusable pieces; in o200k_base, `strawberry` becomes `st | raw | berry`.
The language model processes representations of those pieces and predicts output pieces rather than receiving the word as nine separate alphabet tiles.
The product converts generated pieces back into readable text, which hides the token boundary from the reader.

Because the pieces can contain several letters, exact character operations require the model or surrounding system to recover or inspect detail inside them; the same piece count also governs context capacity and API metering.
explanationArc.earnedClick: The model's fluent paragraph and its letter-counting work are not contradictions: generating likely text from token pieces and explicitly inspecting individual letters are different operations.
explanationArc.smallLanding: When exact letters matter, ask for a character-by-character check or use a tool built to inspect text; when a product quotes a token limit, ask what is included and check the current documentation rather than converting it to a fixed word count.
explanationArc.safetyBoundary: Do not use the strawberry example to claim that all current models fail, that tokenization is the only cause of every character-level error or that every AI model uses this OpenAI encoding.

representativeProofPlan.highestRisk: The rejected tokens section used UTF-8, BPE merge rankings, token IDs, blurry screenshots and a diagram that made the mechanism harder rather than easier. A successor can still fail by hiding the same technical tour behind friendlier sentences or by overstating the viral strawberry example.
representativeProofPlan.plannedProof: After this contract passes, produce only the complete Chapter 2 tokens section, its adjacent deterministic strawberry diagram and its direct Concept Index entry. All are new exact bytes created after this contract. The proof must start from the reader's question, spend its centre on the nontechnical mechanism, connect to context and API metering, state limits and give a precise use move. Do not promote or re-review the predecessor working file. Run exact-prose producer self-review before any role-distinct review.
representativeProofPlan.acceptanceOutcome: An unfamiliar reader can explain, without book wording, why text is divided into variable-sized reusable pieces, why strawberry can be a different task for a language model than for a person looking at letters, why the exact split varies, and how tokens relate to context capacity and API metering. She can apply the idea to an unseen token-window claim and knows what to ask when exact characters matter. The prose and diagram must remain readable, nontechnical, accurate and recognisably LAiDIES.
